**My reasoning:**

I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain. The land here is flat, the soil is decent loam, and the climate gives us two crops a year — that is just the reality of farming here, and I would be a fool to ignore it. The wheat-maize rotation is what this land is made for, and with my education I know how to do it well rather than just going through the motions.

I have about 10 mu of cultivated land. I will run winter wheat followed immediately by summer maize on all of it — sequential double-cropping, no land sitting idle. That is the only system that makes economic sense at this scale.

For wheat, I will use an improved variety from the Jimai series — not traditional seed, which yields poorly, and not full hybrid, which is expensive and less suited to our conditions. I know the groundwater situation in Hebei is serious. I will do three irrigations for wheat — pre-sowing to ensure germination, jointing stage, and heading — and skip the overwintering flood irrigation my father always did. The science is clear that it wastes water without meaningful yield benefit given recent warmer winters.

For fertilizer on wheat, I will split my nitrogen: base application plus topdress at jointing. I got my soil tested two years ago and know I don't need to over-apply phosphorus.

After wheat harvest in June I will direct-seed maize into the stubble. No-till saves me time and money and keeps soil moisture in. Summer rains carry most of the water load for maize — I'll irrigate twice at most, at tasseling and grain fill if rains are short.

I apply pesticides conservatively — herbicide once in spring for wheat, and I scout for corn borer and aphids on maize before deciding whether to spray. Two applications per crop is typical for me.
